title: Reserve chiefs lash Husic on wage rises
full_text:
The Reserve Bank has pushed back on Labor’s suggestion wage growth could outstrip inflation in the absence of productivity gains without piling further pressure on prices, as top officials indicate further rate hikes are imminent.
Fronting the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Economics on Friday, RBA governor Michele Bullock warned that upside risks to the bank’s inflation forecasts appeared to be materialising, while declaring rate rises “do work” in curbing inflation for countries around the world.
The Reserve Bank’s monetary policy board held rates at 4.35 per cent at its August meeting but warned that risks to its inflation forecast were skewed to the upside, with all four major banks now predicting a further 25-basis-point hike by the end of the year.
“Our latest forecasts, which were published with the August Statement on Monetary Policy, suggested that inflation will not return to around the midpoint of the target range until late 2027. Development since then suggests that although growth in the Australian economy is slowing, some of these upside risks to inflation appear to be materialising,” Ms Bullock said.
“It is important that these effects remain contained and do not become embedded into wage- and price-setting decisions. Otherwise, inflation could prove more persistent and require a stronger policy response.” While pointing to global oil and energy price spikes fuelled by persistent conflict in Iran and an artificial intelligence investment boom as key drivers of price growth, Ms Bullock said anaemic productivity was continuing to constrain the economy and pile upward pressure on inflation.
Ms Bullock and deputy governor Andrew Hauser disputed assertions made by the committee’s chair, Labor backbencher Ed Husic, that the RBA would never be satisfied with wage growth outstripping inflation.
“Wages can increase more quickly than inflation … but productivity needs to be there. You can have wages increasing by 3.5 per cent and inflation by 2.5 per cent if you’ve got productivity,” Ms Bullock said.
“We can’t grow much faster, we can’t have faster growth in wages unless productivity picks up. That’s the bottom line.” In the face of deteriorating economic conditions, RBC Capital Markets Sydney head of economics and rates strategy Robert Thompson tipped back-to-back rate hikes in September and November, while ANZ’s Adam Boyton noted a “growing risk of more and earlier hikes”.
“The barrage of recent RBA communication (capped off by a lengthy House Economics Committee appearance today) has left us with little doubt that bank insiders have already made up their minds – a hike in September is the necessary course of action,” Mr Thompson said in a note on Friday.
Ms Bullock said the key question for the monetary policy board when it next meets in just over a week, was whether three interest rate hikes handed down earlier in the year would be sufficient to return inflation to target in a “reasonable time”.
Mr Hauser also pushed back on Mr Husic’s doubt over productivity gains flowing through to workers’ wages.
“Overwhelmingly across time and across countries, countries with higher productivity growth have higher real wages. That is a very robust economic fact,” he told the committee.
“Over the long run, assuming competition, it’s very hard to break that link.” Productivity in Australia is now negative at -0.2 per cent and has been negative or zero for the past three quarters.
The RBA’s warning on lack of productivity growth skewering any chance of wage increases outstripping inflation comes ahead of Jim Chalmers handing down the government’s Intergenerational Report on Monday, which economists expect will include overly “optimistic” productivity forecasts.
Independent research institute e61 urged Labor not to rely on “business-as-usual projections” that risked missing the impact of crises such as the Covid-19 pandemic.
“Major shocks like these have shaped Australia’s past fiscal trajectory, and they won’t stop coming,” e61 senior research economist Aaron Wong said.
“The IGR presents economic projections for the next 40 years, based primarily on how the Treasurer and Treasury believe Australia’s population, participation and productivity will evolve … Heightened global economic and geopolitical uncertainty means that we need to consider a wider range of shocks than just the economic downturns of the past.” E61 modelled a series of potential shocks that could hit the Australian economy, including an escalation of the kind of conflict taking place in the Middle East.
“This could involve events such as import/export restrictions, disruptions to shipping lanes and supply chains, through to military conflict,” Mr Wong said “In addition to the non-economic harms, this would trigger a deep recession in Australia and across the world. This recession would be driven by a collapse in demand for Australian exports, a sharp deterioration in the terms of trade, supply-chain disruption, higher global risk premia and tighter financial conditions.” Other crises e61 urged the government to consider included global bond market shocks following a loss of confidence in the ability of the US to service its debts, or a severe domestic recession characterised by a collapse in external demand and falling commodity prices.
